# Changelog

Every change was tested before and after with headless Copilot CLI runs on public sample apps (JHipster sample app, Spring PetClinic, ThingsBoard, plus small purpose-built apps). Results are counts of runs, so small numbers mean thin evidence.

## Current versions

| Agent | Version | Model |
|---|---|---|
| investigate | v3.20 | GPT-6 Luna |
| implement | v3.16 | GPT-6.1 Sol, fallback GPT-6 Luna |
| review | v3.38 | GPT-6.1 Sol, fallback GPT-6 Luna |
| explain | v1.10 | GPT-6 Luna |
| spec | v1.22 | GPT-6 Luna |
| story (trial) | v1.7 | GPT-6 Luna; subagents use their own models |

## 2026-11-27

- **Workflow controller v1.2 (`tools/story-ctl.py`); code only, no agent change.** (1) **Run log:** every run adds one line to `~/.story-ctl/runs.jsonl` on the developer's machine (outcome, rounds, verdicts, replies, credits per agent, minutes, agent versions); `--stats` summarises it; credits and time so far are shown at each stop and in the final report. Credits of a step killed mid-way are not known and are not counted. (2) **`--report RUN`** writes `problem-report.md` in the shape of the problem-report template: agent versions, criteria, each stop's questions and the reply, each round's verdict line and number of Edit items. (3) **`--resume RUN`** (or `last`) continues a run stopped at a stop, interrupted (Ctrl-C, a closed terminal, a kill), or whose agent step failed twice; finished steps and replies are replayed from a journal written as the run goes, each replayed prompt is checked against the saved one, an interrupted implement step asks before running again over its partial edits, and a finished run is not resumed. Tests: 13 new offline tests (43 in all). Live on GPT-6.1 Sol (st2): a run interrupted 45 seconds into implement with 5 files half changed, resumed with "retry": approved in round 1, hidden acceptance tests 5 of 5, build and frontend tests green, no Copilot process left running; a normal run's log line and problem report matched the run.
- **Workflow controller v1.1 (`tools/story-ctl.py`), from an outside review of the controller; code only, no agent change.** (1) An empty reply, end of input, `stop` or a failed reply command now ends the run at any stop; before, at the handoff it was taken as an answer and implement started. (2) The verdict is read only from a single `- **Verdict:**` line outside code fences; a missing, duplicated or unknown verdict, or Approve with blockers, stops the run instead of starting another implement round. (3) A review with questions always stops for them, even when it repeats the previous round's Edit items (before, the early stop came first), and the repeat check keeps numbers, so a changed limit counts as progress. (4) Investigate, review and explain run with file edits and `git commit`/`push`/`reset`/`checkout`/`stash`/`clean`/`restore` denied, implement with `git push` denied; because a shell command can still write a file (confirmed on the CLI), the controller also compares the working tree before and after each read-only agent and stops if it changed, without reverting anything. (5) A non-zero exit from implement counts as "could not finish"; when an agent returns nothing after changing files it is not retried over the partial edits. (6) Criteria keep their continuation lines (indented, or bulleted under the AC line). (7) `--base` is resolved to a commit at the start, and the state folder works in linked worktrees. (8) Offline tests, `tools/test_story_ctl.py` (30 tests with canned reports, no credits); 24 of them fail on v1.0. The tests also found a v1.0 bug: a second question in a row at the handoff was dropped and the next reply was taken as approval; fixed. Checks: all 201 saved real review reports (40 controller, 161 story agent) give the same verdict with the stricter parser; a Maven verify with Spock specs and the Angular tests leave the working tree unchanged, so the tree check does not stop normal runs.
- **Workflow controller `tools/story-ctl.py` (new, recommended over the story agent):** a small Python script that runs investigate, implement and review as separate Copilot CLI sessions and does the bookkeeping in code: byte-for-byte handoffs and reports, every answer passed to every later task, verdict parsing, round counting, and stops after the handoff and on review questions. A question at a stop is answered by the explain agent and the stop stays open; when implement cannot finish a round (a circuit breaker, a broken build) it stops and asks instead of spending a review; it stops early when a review asks for the same changes as the previous round; each stop opens in VS Code with code links that work from the Markdown preview. Why: the story agent (GPT-6 Luna) made a mechanical mistake (dropped an answer, retyped a report, continued after Approve) in 7 of 45 runs, and on GPT-6.1 Sol it skipped the handoff stop in 4 of 4. Tests: 30 controller story runs with implement and review on Sol had no mechanical failure; same rounds, hidden acceptance tests and credits as the story agent; the new rules passed scripted scenario tests (question at the handoff, circuit breaker then stop, circuit breaker then an instruction, repeated blockers, normal path) and two Sol stories approved in round 1 with every check passing.
- **Repository instructions file (recommended, no agent change):** `.github/copilot-instructions.md` with commands, test levels, layout, conventions and traps. Test (4 stories, implement and review on Sol, graded blind by Claude Opus 5.5): rounds 7 → 5, credits −13%, Opus 7.5 → 7.75. In the same test, tests-first examples at the handoff (7.6, no fewer rounds) and running story and investigate on Sol (story skipped the handoff stop in 4 of 4; 3.4) were not adopted.

- **Tried and not adopted: behavioural invariants across investigate, implement and review** (from an outside review). Investigate listed behaviours that must stay the same with evidence, implement verified each, review judged each and blocked a confirmed break; the workflow controller passed the list to review verbatim. Pre-registered test (implement and review on GPT-6.1 Sol, controller, instruction file, 6 stories with hidden invariant tests, 2 runs per arm): shipped invariant breaks 1 (baseline) vs 2 (candidate) across 8 trap runs; small stories (permissions, paging headers, requests without a version) 0 breaks in both arms; the one real break in both arms was a changed label order in the BANK-401 refactor, which the candidate never listed as an invariant and its review marked "kept". No false blocks on the approved-breaking-change control. Rounds 16 vs 17, credits +10.5%. Not adopted: it prevented nothing the current agents miss. Ordering in large refactors remains the open risk; a recorded contract test before and after a refactor catches it deterministically. In the same test the controller ran 24 stories with no mechanical failure.

- **spec v1.21–v1.22:** three changes from an outside review of the agents, each aimed at a known miss, plus a fix for a regression the first change caused. (1) Before searching, spec lists for itself every need the requirement names or implies (values, inputs, filters, sorts, limits, formats, the user's language and other preferences, empty and error states), decides where each comes from, and looks in our own user, account and settings data for inputs and preferences, not only in downstream responses; every need ends as a mapping row, a requirement or a gap (the list is not added to the reply). (2) It reads each chosen endpoint's success response for errors reported inside HTTP 200 (`ok: false`, an `error` field, an `errors` list) and for partial results, and the Errors line covers those plus a later call failing after an earlier one succeeded, with partial-data handling asked as a business decision. (3) When another team's repository cannot be found or read, fields are "Unable to verify" (missing access is not proof the data does not exist); "Not available anywhere" is kept for sources that show nothing supplies the value. Test (GPT-6 Luna, 2 runs per version per case, graded blind by Claude Opus 5.5 against the sources): email statement case, user's language mapped to the Notification API's locale 0 of 2 → 2 of 2, Opus 6.25 → 8.75; Slack, errors inside HTTP 200 reported 0 of 2 → 2 of 2 (one run explicit, one partial), Opus 4.75 → 8.0; an app ID with no repository and no spec, "Unable to verify" instead of "Not available anywhere" 0 of 2 → 2 of 2, Opus 6.25 → 9.0. Controls: cards 7.0 → 7.5, limits and auth 7.25 → 7.75. Length about 12% longer (about 1,700 → 1,950 words). Wider regression check (Opus blind): revising a spec 5.5 → 8.5 (v1.20 rewrote unchanged parts and dropped the merchant category; v1.21 kept every unchanged row and applied all three changes with half the tool calls, 6–7 vs 14–15, and 0.7 vs 1.0–1.1 credits); FX with a large YAML 7 → 8; Slack in-200 errors 4 of 4 v1.21 runs reported `ok: false`, but only 1 of 4 said outright that it arrives inside HTTP 200. **Regression found and fixed in v1.22:** on the GitHub cases v1.21 scored 5.7 vs 7.0 (h1) and 5.0 vs 7.3 (h2), because listing where each input comes from pushed it to link our customer to their owner record by matching last names (4 of 6 runs vs 1 of 6), using the rule meant for a lookup by email. v1.22 limits that rule to a value that identifies the person or record (email, account or card number); a name is not a link, so the spec says the link is missing and asks how the records connect. After (3 runs each): name-match designs 0 of 6; h1 6.0 vs 6.3, h2 7.7 vs 5.3, cards 8.0 vs 7.0 (the email lookup and the "which card?" question kept). Still missed by every version: the full card number sent in a query string, a missing ownership check on the account endpoint, and the Loyalty member search by email as the way to get a member ID. Also missed by every version: a pet-name validation pattern that differs between the attached spec and the repository.
- **explain v1.10:** at each call to another service or component, explain checks where every input the call needs comes from (the request, the logged-in user, our stored data, configuration, an earlier response) and says so when nothing on the path supplies one, instead of assuming the call works. Test (Luna, 2 runs per version, Opus blind): the Loyalty question, 7 and 6 vs 5 and 6; only v1.10 runs flagged that nothing in our code supplies the member ID (one clearly, one partly). Neither version found the Loyalty member search by email.

## 2026-11-26

- **explain v1.9:** six additions from a review of the template. (1) When the thing asked about does not exist or several places match, it says so and lists the candidates instead of explaining a guess. (2) Read-only GitHub tools (the same three spec uses): it follows a call into another team's code from a local path or from GitHub, and explains an application that is not open in the workspace when given its app ID, repository or name. (3) Markdown documentation can be out of date: the code wins, and the document's claim is named under Couldn't confirm. (4) A **Who can do this** field: roles, permissions and route guards on the path, in the API and the UI. (5) A **Data and calls** field: tables, other services, messages and configuration values with their defaults. (6) Mermaid safety (no semicolons, quote labels with brackets or colons) and links into other repositories (GitHub URL or full local path). Test (GPT-6 Luna, 7 questions on the JHipster sample app, its Loyalty client and the other team's repository, and the public spring-petclinic-rest repository on GitHub, each answered by v1.8 and v1.9, graded blind by Claude Opus 5.5 against the code): v1.9 better on 6, tied on 1; average 8.9 vs 7.0 (8.8 vs 8.0 without the GitHub question). The GitHub-only question: v1.9 9/10 from 38 GitHub file reads, v1.8 1/10 (it could not read the repository and gave up). A feature that does not exist: both said so, v1.9 9 vs 8. A wrong document: both answered from the code; v1.9 also showed that any logged-in user can delete (9 vs 8). v1.8 linked into the other team's repository with relative paths that resolve against our app (broken). Remaining: line ranges sometimes 1–2 lines early (both versions); neither noticed that the Loyalty call needs a member ID our API does not have. About 1 credit per question (2 for the GitHub one).

- **story v1.7 (trial):** the final report's Open items list every handoff question the user did not answer (they replied go, answered only some, or skipped the stop), each with the assumption implement used. Why: on GPT-6.1 Sol, a user who replied "go" got "Approved" with no reminder that the threshold and the sign of the comparison had been decided by assumption; the hidden acceptance tests that encode the analyst's real answers failed 2 of 4. After (configured models): st11 lists the partly answered question and says which parts were assumed ("signed comparison and backfill were not separately confirmed"); st7 lists both unanswered questions with their assumptions. Final versions on the configured models (implement and review on Sol): st7 hidden 7/7 in 2 runs (2 rounds each), st1 4/4 in 1 round, st11 asked about the threshold and the sign (the edge-case rule works on Sol; on Luna it missed the sign) and built the stated assumptions when they were not answered; every automatic check passed except st11's hidden tests for the unanswered points. 35–100 credits per story on Sol.

- **investigate v3.17–v3.20, review v3.36–v3.38: questions keep today's behavior and show options.** Each question is one line: the question, the options and what each means for users or clients, **If unanswered:** the assumption implement will use (for existing behavior, always keep it as today unless a criterion asks for a change), and **Recommendation:** what the agent advises and why, used only if the user agrees. Why: in a Sol story run the user left a question unanswered and implement used the handoff's assumption ("require a version"), which broke older clients; review approved with it as a should-fix. Test (st7 with a user who answers only the first question, plus st2 as a control; GPT-6 Luna; a new hidden test that requests without a version still work): v3.17 (keep-today rule only) kept today's behavior in 2 of 3 handoffs; v3.18 (recommendation next to the assumption) 1 of 3, because both st7 handoffs recommended rejecting and used that as the assumption, and one approved run broke older clients (hidden compatibility test 0/2); v3.19 (assumption first, recommendation separate) 3 of 3, compatibility and version hidden tests 2/2 and 5/5 in all 3 runs, all approved (2, 3 and 3 rounds on Luna). Claude Opus 5.5 judged the format about one point more useful than the assumption-only format when the consequences are filled in, but found about half the recommendations were filler ("clarify", "provide the info"); v3.20 and v3.38 leave the recommendation out when it equals the assumption or the question only asks for information, and keep each question to about 40 words. v3.20 check: all 3 handoffs kept today's behavior as the assumption; Luna still added one information-only recommendation. Open: in st11 neither investigate nor review asked whether a negative amount counts toward the threshold (hidden test 3 of 4). Two v3.20 runs were cut short by a network outage (story retried each failed subagent once, then stopped and named the step, as designed).

- **New test harness (wide story pass):** 10 story shapes on the JHipster sample app (validation, new field, permissions, filter, defect, transaction, locking, contradicting criteria, a vague criterion, a rule only the analyst knows), each with hidden acceptance tests the agents never see; a simulated user (Claude Opus 5.5) answers each stop from a private list of analyst facts in one of three styles (answers what is asked, "go" first then answers, answers only the first question); 12 automatic checks per run (handoff stop, criteria verbatim, every answer carried, round lines, stop on questions, no needless stop, no Met→Can't tell, final copy, read-only agents, no Markdown edits, green build, hidden tests); Opus grades the judgement calls.
- **review v3.34–v3.35, investigate v3.16, story v1.6:** from that pass (GPT-6 Luna, graded by Opus): review held back approval for a second test of behavior a passing test already proved (the edit mode of a form whose create mode was tested; more field assertions than the criterion names) in 4 of 10 stories, 4 extra rounds, and in one story the extra test broke and the story ended not approved; review put a technical suggestion under Questions, which caused a needless stop; investigate wrote open edge cases (a missing version, an unknown id) under risks instead of asking, and in one story guessed wrong; "AC2 is not a requirement, drop it" re-ran investigate and stopped again. Now: review v3.35 calls a criterion Met once a passing test proves each case it names and never asks for the same behavior through another entry point or for assertions on fields the criterion does not name; v3.34 keeps Questions for decisions only the user or analyst can make; investigate v3.16 puts every open point a user or client would notice (an input the criteria do not cover, a value only the analyst knows) under Questions with its assumption; story v1.6 treats removing a criterion as an answer. Before → after on Luna (same stories and reply styles): st1 3 rounds, not approved → 1 round, approved; st5 2 → 1; st10 2 stops → 1; st2 2 → 2; st9 2 → 3 and st7 2 → 3 (both from implement slips on Luna: its own new test failing, a regression); hidden acceptance tests passed in all 16 Luna runs. With implement and review on GPT-6.1 Sol (st1, st7, st10): all approved in round 1, hidden tests pass, every automatic check passes, 22–38 credits per story; Opus 9, 7 and 9 of 10, no false Met, no over-asking. Open: when the user leaves a handoff question unanswered, implement uses the handoff's assumption, and in st7 that assumption ("require a version") broke older clients; review raised it as a should-fix and the final report showed it as the next step.

- **story v1.5 (trial) and review v3.33:** three bugs from real use at work: (1) a review with Request changes and open questions did not stop, so the next round ran without the user's answers; (2) after round 1, story dropped the user's earlier answers from implement and review tasks, so review asked again what was already answered and marked criteria "Can't tell" that an earlier round had Met; (3) after a Needs answers stop the implement task had no "Round n of 3" line. Now an answers rule makes every implement and review task carry an answers block with all of the user's answers so far, oldest first and labelled by stop, a later answer replacing an earlier one on the same point; story stops on Needs answers and on Request changes with questions (showing the Verdict, Questions and Edit), and the next round fixes the Edit items and applies the answers together; every implement task has its round line, and nothing starts after round 3. review v3.33 judges each criterion by its wording plus the user's answers, never asks again what they answer, and never marks "Can't tell" for a point they settle. Test (st7 plus an ambiguous AC4, answers at the handoff): v1.4 reproduced the bug in 1 of 3 runs that went past round 1 (round 2 tasks had 0 of 2 answers; AC4 went from Met to "Can't tell" and the answered question came back); the other two approved in round 1. v1.5, implement and review on GPT-6 Luna: answers in 10 of 10 tasks across 5 rounds, round line on every implement, no repeated questions or "Can't tell"; one approved in 2 rounds, one not approved after 3 because Luna's implement could not make a no-op PUT increment the version (Claude Opus 5.5 confirmed the review's block was correct: 7/10; the approval 8/10). v1.5 with implement and review on GPT-6.1 Sol, "go" at the handoff and only the AC4 question answered later: one round 1 review was Request changes with the AC4 question and story stopped (v1.4 went on); the other was Needs answers and stopped; both approved in round 2, hidden acceptance tests 5/5, green builds; Opus (ran the tests itself): both stops appropriate and answerable from the text shown, both approvals correct, no false Met, no re-asked question, no criterion downgraded, 8/10 each. About 110 credits per Sol story.

## 2026-11-25

- **story v1.4 (trial):** story counts rounds: every implement task starts with "Round n of 3", and after round 3's review it goes straight to the report. Why: a GPT-6 Luna orchestrator ran a 4th round in one st7 run. Not tested separately (a mechanical fix). In the same session, an investigate rule asking handoffs to name framework behaviour that silently skips a case ("every update" vs JPA not bumping `@Version` on a no-op) was tried and dropped: it flagged the trap but resolved it by assuming the lenient reading, and that run took 4 rounds instead of 3.
- **review v3.32:** Needs answers only when a criterion itself is "Can't tell"; a question that comes from a should-fix finding (an unrequested behaviour change, an edge case no criterion names) never stops approval. Why: in a story run, review stopped on "should requests without a version be rejected?" with every criterion met and nothing blocking, which caused a third round and an unneeded stop. Replay of that review (GPT-6 Luna): Approve in 2 of 2 runs, no Edit items. In both runs Luna did not notice the unrequested change at all, so the question was not listed; GPT-6.1 Sol flagged it in its v3.31 review.
- **story v1.3 (trial):** when the handoff stop is skipped ("without stopping"), story adds nothing of its own to implement's task, and the final report's Open items list the handoff's Questions for the analyst, unchanged, with the assumption implement used. At a Needs answers stop it shows the review's Verdict line and Questions field whole, the round number, and asks for answers. Why: graded by Claude Opus 5.5, a v1.2 run added an unlabelled paragraph paraphrasing the criteria and telling implement to use the handoff's assumptions, and the analyst's question never reached the user; the Needs answers stop message was reworded and thin. Test (implement and review on Luna; graded by Opus): st6 approved in 1 round (v1.2 with current agents: 2), 4.7 credits (5.8), hidden acceptance tests 5/5, every report copied whole, the analyst question listed with its assumption; story still added the criteria verbatim and the user's base wording to implement's task (harmless). Current agents through story v1.2 the same day: st6 2 rounds and st7 3 rounds ending at the unneeded Needs answers stop, both hidden 5/5; 1–2 reworded lines per story remain (one review line got a wrong file path).
- **review v3.26–v3.31:** "Met" needs a test line asserting each condition, path or case the criterion names or clearly implies (each method it names, such as PUT and PATCH; for "every" or "all" applied to kinds of calls, each kind, including an update that changes nothing; never the size of a result list). Before asking for a new test, review checks the existing assertions, including tests that change several things at once, and asks only for a condition no assertion would catch; each method the criterion names needs its own assertion, except where one shared mechanism (a class-level transaction, a shared error handler or alert component) enforces the criterion and is already proven. A criterion that keeps behaviour "as today" is proven by unchanged code plus its existing tests. **Edit holds only what a blocker or an unmet criterion needs; should-fix and nit findings never go under Edit**, because implement fixes every Edit item and each extra item costs a round. Unrequested behaviour changes and user decisions go under Questions. No findings that only describe tests; on Approve, Edit is "none". Why: Claude Opus 5.5 regraded saved reviews blind against rebuilt code and found "Met" claims beyond what the cited tests assert and missed gaps; at work, reviews asking for extra tests forced more implement/review cycles on small changes. Test (review replayed on rebuilt code states, graded blind by Opus): v3.25 correct verdict 3 of 6, average 5.8/10, approved the missing "every update" case. v3.27 on Luna 4 of 4, average 8.0, but on GPT-6.1 Sol asked for 5 Edit items where 2 were needed. v3.29–v3.30 asked for exactly the needed items on Luna; on Sol v3.30 caught every required item (including a subtle PATCH-only test Luna missed) with 3 and 2 items instead of 5, each review still adding one test through an already-proven shared mechanism, which v3.31 addresses. v3.31 on Luna: control still blocks a changed existing test, "as today" approved with no Edit items, "every update" blocked with exactly the 2 needed items. v3.31 on Sol (graded by Opus): the extra items are gone. The PATCH case got exactly its 1 required test (9/10, rounds equal to ideal, v3.30: 6/10 with about 6 extra rollback tests), and "every update" got the 2 required items plus one arguable form test (7/10, v3.30: 6/10 with a heavy real-HTTP test; v3.27: 5 items); known Luna miss: a PATCH test that also moves the account was taken as proving the same-account change.
- **investigate v3.14–v3.15:** one Edit line per changed method or block, with a range from its annotations or signature through its closing brace (never the class header or the whole file); Ripple names traps the implementer will hit (state a save or merge overwrites before it is read, test transactions that hide rollback or version behaviour unless flushed). Why: Opus found 2 of 3 recent st6 handoffs had Edit ranges too narrow (only the class header) or the whole file, so implement, which opens only those ranges, could miss whole methods. Test (Luna, Opus blind): implement-readiness v3.12–v3.13 average 5.8 → v3.14 7.75 → v3.15 8; range precision 4.7 → 8.5 → 9.5 (v3.15 ranges end on the closing brace; v3.14 often stopped 1–3 lines short). st7: only v3.14+ handoffs named the fixtures that break and the flush needed. Still missed by all: that a request's related entity is an id-only reference that must be loaded.
- **Confirmed by Opus regrade (no prompt change):** review v3.23 test-edit rule (v3.22 got 1 of 4 right, v3.23 4 of 4, legitimate test edits approved 4 of 4); markdown rules (review breaches 1 of 4 → 0 of 4; investigate docs under Edit 2 of 2 → 0 of 3); Luna default effort for investigate (medium and high both 15 of 15 on the security audit).
- **spec v1.20:** four fixes from blind grading by Claude Opus 5.5 (graders saw anonymised outputs, checked every claim against the source files, and did not know which version wrote what). (1) When the only documented way to get a required input can return several matches (a card lookup by email), spec uses it and asks how to choose, instead of rejecting it and leaving the input unresolved: chain used and "which card?" asked in 6/6 runs (v1.19: 0/2; v1.14–v1.18: 14 of 15 used it). (2) The Not stated line gives one owner per topic. (3) A declared `security` wins over scopes named in a parameter description, and a difference is reported (one v1.19 Slack run took the wrong scope from the description). (4) A conflict between what our client sends and what another team requires is always a question to that team. Opus scores, limits/auth correctness and how actionable the analyst's asks are (1–10): Slack 9 and 7 (v1.19: 9/4 and 5/4; v1.16: 6/3); limits case 10 and 8 (v1.19: 10/4 and 10/6; v1.16: 4/3). Card mapping 7–8 of 10 (v1.19: 4 and 4). Opus also graded v1.19 against v1.16 on 9 cases: limits case 14, 14 vs 6 of 14; Slack 8.5, 10.5 vs 8 of 11; FX 7.5 vs 6.5; others equal within half a point except the card cases (fixed in v1.20); every output without a limits section was v1.16; writing judged about equal (v1.19 ahead on 4 of 6 cases) and more usable, because auth and limits appear where an analyst looks. Revising a v1.19-format spec: 8 and 9 of 10 (one revision dropped a sentence and under-reported its changes). Regression check (one v1.20 run per case type, graded blind by Opus against v1.19 and v1.16): current Swagger 5, 5, 5 of 5; stale Swagger 6 (v1.19 5.5, v1.16 6) of 6; GitHub-only lookup 4.5 for all three; FX from the repository 7 (v1.19 7, v1.16 6.5) of 8; FX attached 7.5 (v1.19 7.5, v1.16 7) of 8; email 8 (v1.16 8.5 and 8) of 9; revising a v1.19 spec 8.5 (v1.19 7) of 10. Every v1.20 and v1.19 output had an accurate non-functional section; every output without one was v1.16. Wrong facts in v1.20: none, apart from two line ranges a few lines off. Still open: rate limits that a spec doesn't state are listed but rarely asked of a single team; some unknowns still name two teams; no version rejects the same-named but wrong GitHub repository by name (all pick the right one); none maps the email locale to our stored user language.
- **spec v1.19:** shorter Non-functional requirements: one short line per need that the UI team states, a downstream team documents or our code sets, then one **Not stated:** line with who should answer; those topics are no longer repeated under Decisions and questions or Risks. A revised spec's header shows the agent's version (one v1.18 revision wrote "v1.17" by bumping the previous spec's number). Why: in a blind writing judge (GPT-6 Luna, analyst section only, both orders, 4 cases) v1.16 beat v1.18 in 6 of 8 comparisons, with concision 7.75 vs 6.0; the new section added about 170 words and the same gaps were said up to three times. After: concision 7.0 vs 7.0, judge 3–5 (it reversed its pick between orders on two cases), total length 1,375–1,671 words vs 1,580–1,750 for v1.16, both revision headers correct.
  - **Final check across every case type (v1.18 and v1.19 against v1.16):** an independent case on Slack's public Web API spec (1.2 MB, 174 endpoints, not written for this test): 10/14 → 13, 13, 13/14, including the declared scope `channels:history`, the spec's own scope disagreement (`conversations:history` in the token description), and "not stated" for rate limits and timeouts, with 0 invented rate limits, `Retry-After` headers or page maximums (Slack documents rate tiers elsewhere, not in this spec). Planted limits case 13/13 facts. FX case 7 → 8, 7/8; card case 7–8/9 (unchanged); stale and current Swagger, GitHub-only lookup, attached JSON and 120 KB YAML: same differences caught. Revision: rows kept 4/4 in all 3 runs. Known small issues: about 1 link in 50 has a line range one past the end of the file (it still opens the file); Slack's errors arriving as HTTP 200 with `ok: false` were noted by v1.16 but not by v1.18 or v1.19; the email case's language field is raised as a question but not mapped to our stored user language.
- **spec v1.18:** **Limits, auth and timeouts** looks in three places, with a source link after each item: (1) their spec, attached, pasted or in their repository (`securitySchemes` and each operation's `security`, page and size `maximum` and `default`, cursors, `429` and rate-limit or `Retry-After` headers, `Cache-Control`/`ETag`, `x-` extensions; an `example` value is reported as "example only, limit not stated"); (2) their code and configuration (security config and scopes, paging limits, rate limiters); (3) our client and its properties (timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, caching, the credentials it sends). Disagreements, such as our client sending an API key where their service requires an OAuth scope, go under Mismatches and gaps. New test case: a points and offers screen with 13 facts planted across an attached Offers Swagger, the Loyalty repository's code and our Loyalty client. Found: v1.16 6/13 → v1.18 13/13 in 4 of 4 final runs (grader misses on wordings such as "2/5 seconds" and "3,000 ms" checked by hand). Source links on that line: 0/2 runs → 2/2 after naming the link rule there. "600 per minute" from an `example` stated as a limit: 2/4 → 0/2 after the example clause. 0 invented targets; 51 of 52 links valid (one line range one past the end of a file). Email case 8, 8 of 9 (v1.16) → 8, 7 (one run left out the 5 MB attachment limit). Credits per run 1.3 → 1.5–1.9 on the new case.
- **spec v1.17:** four changes, tested on GPT-6 Luna against v1.16 (1 run per revision case for v1.16, 2 for v1.17; 2–3 runs per regression case).
  - **Revising a spec:** paste "Previous spec:" plus the changes (a changed requirement, answers or corrections). spec keeps unaffected parts word for word, re-reads only the sources the changes touch, and adds "What changed since the previous spec". An added requirement (50 instead of 20 authorizations, plus card last four digits and merchant category): unchanged mapping rows kept 1/4 → 4/4, credits 0.84 → 0.69 and 0.49, tool calls 20 → 9 and 3. Answers to questions (deployed Swagger confirmed, visits newest first): rows kept 0/5 → 4/5 (the fifth changed because of the answer), credits 2.27 → 1.16 and 0.89 (a fresh spec costs 2.4–3.0), tool calls 49 → 9 and 5. "What changed" present 0/2 → 4/4. One run kept an answered question in place, marked "confirmed", instead of removing it.
  - **Functional and non-functional requirements:** "What the UI team asked for" is now **Functional requirements**, followed by **Non-functional requirements** (NFR1, NFR2, ...): response time and volume, freshness and caching, behaviour when another team's service is slow or down, who may see the data and what must be masked or kept out of logs, audit. Each is stated, documented by a downstream team, or "not stated: ask <who>"; targets are never invented. The engineer section adds **Limits, auth and timeouts** per downstream call. Present in 8/8 runs, with 0 invented response-time figures; documented limits were used (for example the Cards service's maximum of 100 per request).
  - **Missed fields:** before replying, spec checks that every value, filter, sort, limit and format the requirement names or implies has a row or a gap line. On the email case, the email language was raised as a question in 2/2 runs (v1.16: 1/2), but still not mapped to our stored user language in any run (0/4 for both versions).
  - **Links and length:** link targets come from the path or URL the file was opened with, never from file text, with no spaces or backslashes; Mapping sources no longer repeats the table, and rejected endpoints get a few words each. Broken local links on the card case: 1/3 → 0/2 runs (too few runs to call it fixed); 1 link of 18 in one run had a line range one past the end of the file. Length about 1,750 → 1,850 words on average (the new requirements section, partly offset by the trims).
  - **No regressions:** card case 8, 8, 7 of 9 → 8, 8 of 9; stale-spec case (attached vs repository differences, visit-date flag, GitHub lookups) and attached-JSON case unchanged.

## 2026-11-24

- **implement v3.16:** before reporting, implement checks each acceptance criterion the way review judges it: the test asserts the behaviour itself, would fail without it and passed in its run (an existing test counts only if implement read its assertions), and every case the wording names or clearly implies has one (each method, endpoint or field it names, error and boundary cases, each kind of call for "every" or "all"); no tests for cases the wording does not cover. Why: round 1 was sent back in 8 of 8 story runs, every time for a case the wording implies without a test (or with a failing one), and the same happened in real use at work on GPT-6.1 Sol. The old rule was only "make sure each AC has a test that proves it". After (GPT-6 Luna, through story): st6 approved in round 1 in 2 of 2 runs (before 0 of 2), 4.7 credits each (before 5.5–6.2); st7 still 2 rounds in 2 of 2, round 1 failing on an existing test's teardown that the new `@Version` broke, not on a missing test; hidden acceptance tests 5/5 and green builds in all 4. Wider check (one run per version per story): st2 (IBAN) 1 round and 5.1 credits (before 3 rounds and 10.9, round 1 sent back for a missing form test); st4 (filter) 2 rounds and 7.6 credits (before 1 round and 4.6), round 1 sent back for a code slip (labels not loaded when filtering), not a test; tests added stayed within the wording (6 and 3, before 7 and 2); green builds in all 4. Across the 6 v3.16 runs, no round 1 failed for inadequate tests (before 9 of 10).
- **story v1.2 (trial):** replies at the handoff stop. Answers to the handoff's questions (with or without go) now go straight to implement and to every later review as "Answers from the user (verbatim):"; only an explicit request to change the plan, or a changed criterion, runs investigate again, and then with the previous handoff included. A new Stops rule: story never skips the handoff stop by assuming answers to analyst questions, only when the user's message says "without stopping", and never skips the Needs answers stop. Why: in real use, an answers-only reply at the stop re-ran investigate from scratch (v1.1 had only "go" or "changes"); and in testing the handoff stop held in only 3 of 6 v1.0/v1.1 runs (0 of 3 on one afternoon), with story reasoning that it could "reasonably assume" the analyst answers. After (GPT-6 Luna): stop held 8 of 8; answers-only reply went straight to implement 3 of 3 (a first wording that said "changes to the plan" without the default still re-ran investigate 1 of 1); plan change re-ran investigate with the previous handoff 35/35 lines and stopped again 2 of 2, at about 1 credit instead of 2.3; full chain with an answers reply: answers in all 4 later tasks, AC4 Met from the first review with no second Needs answers, approved in 2 rounds, hidden 5/5, green build, about 14 credits.
- **story v1.1 (trial):** a copying rule: every report is passed on and shown whole, from its `#` header to its last line, including "For implement"; the handoff stop shows the whole handoff; the Needs answers task carries the whole review plus "Answers from the user (verbatim):"; every subagent start has a description. Why: a line-by-line check of v1.0 runs (each subagent's real output against what the orchestrator passed on) found the orchestrator retypes reports and trims them: the handoff stop showed rewritten fields without code links; the review's whole "For implement" section was dropped from the Needs answers task and from the final reply (2 of 2 runs that reached it); and the first subagent start failed with `"description": Required` in 2 of 4 runs. After (GPT-6 Luna, 2 runs): handoff stop 37/37 lines unchanged; Needs answers review passed whole with the answer verbatim; final reply carried the last review whole, "For implement" included, in 2/2; no start failures. Still retyped, not copied: 1 or 2 lines per run differ by a word or a character (once a reworded table row, once a wrong path in a context link). Criteria verbatim in every review in every run (v1.0 and v1.1). Results: interactive run (handoff stop, "go", Needs answers, answer) approved after 3 rounds, hidden 5/5, about 13 credits; BANK-401 refactor on v1.0, 3 rounds, not approved (review wanted the full suite run), structural 14/14, contract 34/35 (Luna chains without story: 20–21/35), 15.5 credits. VS Code check: subagents run with their own agent file's model and fresh context, but use the effort picked for story.
- **story v1.0 (new, trial):** orchestrator that runs investigate, implement and review as subagents. Its only tool starts subagents; it keeps the acceptance criteria from the user's message and passes them verbatim to every review, stops after the handoff for "go", stops on Needs answers, and allows at most 3 rounds. Copilot CLI checks: each subagent used the model in its own agent file and started with fresh context (it could not see the orchestrator's instructions). Two stories on GPT-6 Luna: both approved in 2 rounds, hidden acceptance tests 5/5, green builds, criteria verbatim in 4 of 4 reviews; 6.2 and 8.2 credits per story, of which the orchestrator used 0.7–0.8 (about 10%).
- **implement v3.15:** the report's first field is always **Acceptance criteria**: every criterion from the story, handoff or review, verbatim and in order, including ones the round didn't touch, each with the test that proves it; "none given" when there were none. Luna: 3 of 3 criteria verbatim in all 3 reports of a 3-round chain; a defect without criteria wrote "none given".
- **explain v1.8, spec v1.16:** read-only by design: the terminal tool is removed, so they can only read and search (spec also keeps its read-only GitHub tools). Tested on GPT-6 Luna against the previous versions: explain citations 72/72 → 70/70 valid on 3 questions; spec mappings, warnings and stale-spec differences unchanged on 7 runs (stale attached spec, attached JSON, repository only), all links valid except one run that broke 16 local-file links with a stray space (1 of 3 runs on that case; not seen on GitHub or attached-file links).
- **investigate v3.13, review v3.25:** they keep the terminal (git and one test run) but run Maven tests with the frontend skip flags (in 1 of 637 earlier read-only steps a test run without them rewrote `package-lock.json`), and run `git status --short` at the start and end, reporting any file a command changed. Two Luna chains: skip flags on every test run, no file changed by either agent, hidden tests 5/5.
- **investigate v3.12, implement v3.14, review v3.24:** Markdown files (`*.md`) are generated by a separate documentation agent, so the coding agents only read them. investigate no longer lists docs under Edit or Ripple, implement never creates or edits `*.md` (and skips one if a handoff or review lists it), and review never asks for documentation changes; a criterion that asks only for documentation is left to the documentation agent. Tested on a sample app with API docs the stories make out of date (all GPT-6 Luna, 2 runs per story): implement edited a doc in 2/4 chains before, 0/4 after; review asked for doc fixes in 1/4 replays before (on a repo whose README says to keep the docs in sync), 0/4 after. Hidden acceptance tests 5/5 and green builds in every run, before and after; review rounds 7 before, 5 after.

## 2026-11-23

Refactor that added a rule to an existing architecture test, against a criterion forbidding test edits: Sol blocked it 0/2 → 2/2 (before, it called the edit "additive"), Luna 1/2 → 2/2. Four correct changes, two of them with legitimate test edits, still approved 4/4.

If the repository can't be found, map from the attachment and say so. Before → after: repository checked with a file attached 3/6 → 6/6; stale attached file caught and questioned 1/2 → 2/2; no regressions on 4 earlier cases.
